name: LM25119QPSQX_NOPB
title: Dual synchronous buck controller, 4.5 V to 42 V input
summary: The LM25119 is a two-channel synchronous step-down controller for 4.5 V to 42 V inputs that drives external high-side and low-side N-channel MOSFETs with 3.3 A peak gate drive and adaptive dead time. It uses emulated peak current mode control, so it handles very small duty cycles at high input voltage, and it can run as two outputs or as one output from two interleaved phases. Frequency is set from 50 kHz to 750 kHz per channel or synchronised; soft-start, UVLO, current limit with hiccup, diode emulation, switch-over to an external bias supply and thermal shutdown are built in. It comes in a 5 mm × 5 mm 32-pin WQFN with exposed pad.
key_figures: 4.5 V to 42 V (45 V absolute maximum)

pins.name: VCC1
pins.function: Output of the channel 1 bias regulator (7.6 V); feeds the channel 1 controller and the low-side driver, and charges the HB1 bootstrap capacitor through an external diode. Decouple to ground with a ceramic capacitor at the pin.

pins.name: LO1
pins.function: Channel 1 low-side gate drive. Route to the synchronous MOSFET gate over a short, low-inductance path.

pins.name: PGND1
pins.function: Return of the channel 1 low-side driver. Tie it straight to the grounded end of the channel 1 sense resistor.

pins.name: CSG1
pins.function: Kelvin ground of the channel 1 current-sense amplifier; runs on its own trace to the grounded end of the channel 1 sense resistor.

pins.name: CS1
pins.function: Channel 1 current-sense amplifier input, taken from the upper (MOSFET) end of the channel 1 sense resistor.

pins.name: RAMP1
pins.function: Channel 1 PWM ramp. A resistor from SW1 and a capacitor to AGND set its slope so that it mimics the inductor current.

pins.name: SS1
pins.function: Channel 1 soft-start. An internal 10 µA source charges the capacitor on this pin and the error amplifier follows that voltage up to 0.8 V. Held low while either VCC is under 4 V, while UVLO is under 1.25 V, or in thermal shutdown; pulling it to AGND turns channel 1 off.

pins.name: VCCDIS
pins.function: Above 1.25 V it turns both internal VCC regulators off so the VCC pins can be fed from outside through a diode. An internal 500 kΩ pull-down keeps the regulators on when the pin is open; a divider from the external bias rail can override it.

pins.name: FB1
pins.function: Inverting input of the channel 1 error amplifier. A divider from the channel 1 output sets the output; the regulation point is 0.8 V.

pins.name: COMP1
pins.function: Output of the channel 1 error amplifier. The compensation network goes from this pin to FB1. In one-output interleaved use it also drives channel 2 through a tie to COMP2.

pins.name: EN2
pins.function: Channel 2 enable. Below 2 V channel 2 stops while channel 1 and everything else keep running; above 2.5 V it runs. A 50 kΩ internal pull-up enables channel 2 when the pin is open.

pins.name: AGND
pins.function: Analog ground: return of the 0.8 V reference and the analog circuits.

pins.name: RT
pins.function: Oscillator set pin. One resistor to AGND sets the frequency; the oscillator runs at twice the per-channel switching frequency, up to a recommended 1.5 MHz (750 kHz per channel). A positive pulse coupled in through a small capacitor synchronises it to an external clock.

pins.name: RES
pins.function: Hiccup restart timer. After 256 consecutive current-limited cycles on either channel, that channel stops and a 10 µA source charges the capacitor on this pin; at 1.25 V the channel restarts. The channels act on overload independently. Tied to VCC at first power-up, hiccup mode is disabled.

pins.name: COMP2
pins.function: Output of the channel 2 error amplifier; its compensation network runs between it and FB2. When FB2 is tied to VCC2 this output goes high-impedance and is joined to COMP1.

pins.name: FB2
pins.function: Inverting input of the channel 2 error amplifier; a divider from the channel 2 output sets it, regulating at 0.8 V. Tied to VCC2 it disables the channel 2 error amplifier for interleaved operation.

pins.name: DEMB
pins.function: Diode-emulation select. Low (or open, through a 50 kΩ internal pull-down) turns diode emulation on: the low-side MOSFET is held off for the rest of the cycle once the inductor current reverses. High lets current flow both ways in the low-side MOSFET.

pins.name: SS2
pins.function: Channel 2 soft-start, the same as SS1: a capacitor charged by an internal 10 µA source sets the reference ramp. Held low while either VCC is under 4 V, while UVLO is under 1.25 V, or in thermal shutdown; pulling it to AGND turns channel 2 off.

pins.name: RAMP2
pins.function: Channel 2 PWM ramp, set by a resistor from SW2 and a capacitor to AGND.

pins.name: CS2
pins.function: Channel 2 current-sense amplifier input, from the upper end of the channel 2 sense resistor.

pins.name: CSG2
pins.function: Kelvin ground of the channel 2 current-sense amplifier, to the grounded end of the channel 2 sense resistor.

pins.name: PGND2
pins.function: Return of the channel 2 low-side driver; tie it straight to the grounded end of the channel 2 sense resistor.

pins.name: LO2
pins.function: Channel 2 low-side gate drive; short, low-inductance path to the synchronous MOSFET gate.

pins.name: VCC2
pins.function: Output of the channel 2 bias regulator (7.6 V); supplies the channel 2 low-side driver and bootstrap diode. Decouple to ground with a ceramic capacitor at the pin.

pins.name: SW2
pins.function: Channel 2 switch node: high-side source, low-side drain and the lower end of the channel 2 bootstrap capacitor.

pins.name: HO2
pins.function: Channel 2 high-side gate drive; short, low-inductance path to the high-side MOSFET gate.

pins.name: HB2
pins.function: Supply of the channel 2 high-side driver. Connects to the bootstrap diode cathode and the bootstrap capacitor, which sits right at the IC and supplies the gate charge.

pins.name: UVLO
pins.function: Line undervoltage lockout. Below 0.4 V the part is shut down; between 0.4 V and 1.25 V it is in standby with the VCC regulators on, soft-start pins held low and no switching; above 1.25 V switching starts and a 20 µA source turns on into the external divider for hysteresis. Never leave it open.

pins.name: VIN
pins.function: Supply input of the two VCC regulators.

pins.name: HB1
pins.function: Supply of the channel 1 high-side driver: bootstrap diode cathode and bootstrap capacitor, the capacitor placed right at the IC.

pins.name: HO1
pins.function: Channel 1 high-side gate drive; short, low-inductance path to the high-side MOSFET gate.

pins.name: SW1
pins.function: Channel 1 switch node: high-side source, low-side drain and the lower end of the channel 1 bootstrap capacitor.

pins.name: EP
pins.function: Exposed thermal pad, with no electrical connection inside. Solder it to the ground plane to lower thermal resistance.

circuits.title: Typical application circuit
circuits.description: Two independent synchronous buck channels from one input. Each channel has a high-side and a low-side N-channel MOSFET driven from HO and LO, a bootstrap diode and capacitor from VCC to HB across SW, a sense resistor in the low-side source read by CS and CSG, an RC from the switch node that builds the emulated current ramp, a divider into FB and a series RC with a parallel capacitor from FB to COMP. A divider from VIN sets the UVLO level; single capacitors set soft-start and the restart timer, and one resistor sets the frequency.
notes: DEMB, EN2 and VCCDIS are not connected; open, they leave diode emulation on, channel 2 enabled and the internal VCC regulators running.

circuits.title: 3.3 V 8 A and 1.8 V 8 A dual-output application
circuits.description: The evaluation board run as two outputs from 6 V to 36 V at 230 kHz: channel 1 makes 3.3 V and channel 2 makes 1.8 V, each up to 8 A, with SI7884 MOSFETs, 6.8 µH inductors and 8 mΩ sense resistors. R1 and C9 filter the VIN pin; R2, R3 and C8 set UVLO turn-on at about 5.6 V with 1.05 V of hysteresis. R4 (22.1 kΩ) sets the frequency and TP1 couples a sync clock into RT through C10. Each channel has a 34 kΩ / 820 pF ramp network, a 10 Ω / 1000 pF filter on CS and CSG, a 5.1 Ω / 1000 pF snubber on the switch node and a 680 µF electrolytic plus ceramics at the output. The feedback dividers include 10 Ω resistors with test points for loop measurement. Parts marked NU are not fitted: an external bias input through D3, D4 and the VCCDIS divider R35/R36, the DEMB pull-up R16, the EN2 pull-down R5, and the interleave links R21 and R22.

parts.note: VCCDIS divider top, from the external bias

notes: NU marks a position that is not fitted.
A link marked SINGLE OUTPUT sits between OUTPUT1 and OUTPUT2; it is open for two outputs.
PGND1, PGND2, AGND and the exposed pad all go to GND; the Kelvin traces CSG1 and CSG2 (through R32 and R31) end at the grounded side of R18 and R20.

circuits.title: Two-phase interleaved 3.3 V 16 A application
circuits.description: The same board turned into one 3.3 V, 16 A output with two interleaved phases. R22 (0 Ω) ties FB2 to VCC2 so the channel 2 error amplifier is off and COMP2 is high-impedance; R21 (0 Ω) joins COMP2 to COMP1 so channel 1's amplifier and its 36.5 kΩ / 6800 pF / 100 pF network drive both phases. The channel 2 compensation (R6, C15, C14) and the channel 2 divider (R9, R12, R13) are removed, and the two outputs are joined into one.

parts.note: VCCDIS divider top, from the external bias

notes: NU marks a position that is not fitted.
The two power stages carry identical parts.

circuits.title: VCC bias from an extra winding on the output inductor
circuits.description: For outputs below 5 V, a second winding on the output inductor stacked on top of VOUT, through a diode, gives a bias voltage that feeds VCC. The capacitor holds VCC against VOUT. With VCCDIS taken above 1.25 V the internal regulators stop and VCC comes from this supply.

parts.note: added winding on the L1A core; dotted end at the diode

notes: The dotted end of the main winding is at SW.

circuits.title: Feedback and compensation network
circuits.description: RFB2 from the output and RFB1 to ground divide the output onto FB, where it is held at 0.8 V. RCOMP in series with CCOMP from COMP to FB forms the Type II network; CHF across them adds a high-frequency pole.
notes: Channel 2 is the same on FB2 and COMP2.

circuits.title: UVLO divider
circuits.description: RUV2 from VIN and RUV1 to ground set the input voltage at which UVLO crosses 1.25 V; the internal 20 µA source switched into the divider at that point sets the hysteresis. CFT filters the pin.

operation.text: Dual synchronous buck controller for 4.5 V to 42 V inputs, driving external N-channel MOSFETs on both channels. Control is peak current mode built on an emulated current ramp, giving line feedforward, cycle-by-cycle current limit and simple compensation, and allowing very short on-times at high input voltage. The two channels can make two separate outputs or one high-current output from two interleaved phases. Frequency is set by one resistor from 50 kHz to 750 kHz per channel, or locked to an external clock.

The LM25119 comes in one 32-pin WQFN (RTV) package, 5 mm × 5 mm, with an exposed pad. The orderable parts LM25119PSQ/NOPB, LM25119PSQE/NOPB and LM25119PSQX/NOPB differ only in reel size (1000, 250 and 4500 pieces).

Two internal high-voltage regulators, VCC1 and VCC2, each set to 7.6 V, supply the controllers and gate drivers of their channels; VIN can be fed directly from up to 42 V. Below the set point VCC follows VIN less a small dropout. Each regulator is limited to 25 mA minimum. When both VCC pins pass 4 V and UVLO is above 1.25 V, both channels enable and soft-start begins; they run until a VCC pin drops below 3.8 V, UVLO drops below 1.25 V or the die overheats. An undervoltage on VCC1 also disables channel 2, which keeps channel 2 from running open-loop in interleaved mode; either VCC in undervoltage stops both channels.

At high input voltage the regulator dissipation can be large, so VCC may be fed from a supply derived from the output. VCCDIS above 1.25 V switches the internal regulators off; the external bias has to be fed into the VCC pins via a diode, ideally a low-drop Schottky. The 500 kΩ internal pull-down keeps the regulators on with nothing connected, and a divider from the bias supply can lift VCCDIS. The pass transistor has a diode from VCC to VIN that must stay reverse-biased: if the bias can exceed VIN, put a blocking diode from the input supply to VIN. For outputs from 5 V to 14.5 V the output can feed VCC through a diode; below 5 V an added winding on the output inductor serves.
VIN must not exceed its 45 V absolute maximum; ringing on the input line during line or load steps can damage the part. Good layout and quality bypass capacitors close to VIN and AGND are needed.

UVLO has two levels. Below 0.4 V the part is shut down, with 100 mV of hysteresis on that comparator. Between 0.4 V and 1.25 V it is in standby: the VCC regulators run but the outputs stay off, so the pin can serve as a remote enable. Above 1.25 V, with both VCC pins above 4 V, switching begins. A divider from VIN sets the minimum operating input; when the pin crosses 1.25 V an internal 20 µA source turns on into the divider and lifts the pin, and when it falls back the source turns off, which gives the hysteresis. The pin must not float. An open-drain or open-collector transistor pulling UVLO below 0.4 V shuts the part down. The UVLO pin must stay below 15 V; a clamp may be needed at high input voltages.

EN2 below 2 V shuts channel 2 down while channel 1 continues; above 2.5 V channel 2 runs. The internal 50 kΩ pull-up means the pin may be left open. Holding EN2 low while UVLO rises lets channel 1 start alone; both run once UVLO, EN2, VCC1 and VCC2 are all above their thresholds. Either channel can also be turned off by grounding its SS pin.

A resistor from RT to AGND, placed close to the IC with direct connections, sets the frequency. The oscillator runs at twice the per-channel frequency and a divider splits it into two channels 180° apart at the HO pins. To synchronise, AC-couple a positive edge into RT: the pin sits at 1.25 V nominal and must be driven above 4 V to trigger the sync detector; a 5 V pulse through 100 pF is recommended. Each channel switches at half the applied sync frequency. Syncing above twice the free-running frequency can upset the modulator.

Each channel has a high-gain error amplifier comparing its FB pin with a 0.8 V reference; its output is brought out on COMP for the compensation network. A Type II network is the usual choice: a pole at zero frequency, a zero in mid-band and a noise-cutting pole at high frequency. Each PWM comparator sets the duty cycle by comparing the emulated current against COMP.

For one output from two phases only the channel 1 amplifier is used. Tie FB2 to VCC2: the channel 2 amplifier turns off and COMP2 goes high-impedance. Join COMP1 and COMP2 at the IC so channel 2 follows channel 1 and the phases share current, put the compensation between FB1 and the joined COMP pins, and tie the outputs of the two power stages to each other at the output capacitor bank. Size each phase for half the output current.

Rather than measuring the high-side switch current, which carries a leading-edge spike and measurement delay that limit the minimum pulse width, the part rebuilds the current signal from two pieces. The DC level comes from sampling the voltage across the sense resistor in the low-side path, held just before the high-side switch turns on. The rising slope comes from an external capacitor from RAMP to AGND charged through a resistor from SW. Connecting the resistor to SW, not VIN, keeps the RAMP pin within its rating and gives slope compensation that scales with VIN, so no other slope circuit is needed. CRAMP must be below 2 nF so the internal switch can discharge it every cycle; a stable ceramic of 5 % or better is recommended.

If the inductor ripple does not settle back to its starting value by the next cycle, alternating wide and narrow pulses appear at the switch node. The ramp equations give the optimum slope compensation; more can be added by lowering RRAMP or CRAMP. K between 1 and 3 trades cross-talk, short-circuit peak current, inductor size, sense-resistor loss and efficiency; below 1 sub-harmonic oscillation can occur, and above 3 an extra pole appears near crossover.

The emulated current follows the switch current, scaled by the sense resistor and the ×10 sense amplifier. When it exceeds 1.2 V the cycle ends. With small inductance and high input voltage the current can overshoot because of comparator delay; the sample-and-hold then sees the excess valley current before the next turn-on and, while it stays above the limit, the high-side switch is skipped until the current decays. This stops runaway from delay or inductor saturation. With the output shorted at maximum input, the high-side MOSFET is held off until the valley current has fallen under VCS(TH) / RS.

A counter tracks cycles that end in current limit. After 256 in a row on one channel, that channel stops switching (HO and LO off) and stays off while a 10 µA source charges the RES capacitor to 1.25 V, then restarts. The channels act independently, so one can hiccup while the other runs. The RES setting is latched at first power-up once UVLO is above 1.25 V and both VCC pins are above their thresholds: RES tied to VCC then disables hiccup mode.

The error amplifier regulates FB to whichever is lower, the SS voltage or 0.8 V. From SS = 0 V an internal 10 µA source charges the SS capacitor, so FB and the output rise gradually. Grounding an SS pin disables its channel.

operation.topic: Gate drivers, bootstrap and dead time
operation.text: Each channel has a high-current high-side driver with level shift, powered from a bootstrap capacitor on HB that charges from VCC through an external diode while SW is low; use 0.1 µF or more of ceramic with short traces from HB to SW. At high duty cycle the high-side switch is forced off for 320 ns every cycle to recharge the bootstrap capacitor and to sample the low-side current. Adaptive dead time keeps HO and LO from ever being on together: HO turns on a short delay after the LO voltage has fallen, and LO waits for HO to discharge, whatever the MOSFET size.

If VCC comes from the output, or the input can be low at start, the MOSFET threshold must be below the 4 V VCC undervoltage level. Otherwise the gates may not be fully driven when VCC lockout releases, and the converter may fail to start or hang briefly in a high-dissipation state. A lower-threshold MOSFET, or VCC from a source above the output, avoids it; it does not arise when the UVLO divider sets the minimum input above the VCC regulation level.
The 320 ns forced off-time limits the duty cycle, more so at high frequency. Check the needed maximum duty cycle, losses included, against DMAX = 1 - fSW × 320 ns.
At about 165 °C junction temperature the part enters a low-power reset: the drivers and the VCC regulators are turned off. The shutdown threshold has 25 °C of hysteresis.

A synchronous buck with a low-side MOSFET can draw current back from the output at light load, in overvoltage or when starting into a pre-biased output. With diode emulation on, the low-side MOSFET turns off when reverse current is detected (SW zero-cross threshold about -5 mV). That lowers loss at light and no load, permits discontinuous conduction, and allows start-up into a pre-biased output without discharging it; the cost is slower light-load transient response. Diode emulation is recommended. DEMB grounded or open enables it; for continuous conduction tie DEMB to VCC1 or VCC2 (above 2.6 V).

operation.topic: Pin settings in the design example
operation.text: EN2 is left open so channel 2 always runs; pulling it below 2 V stops channel 2. DEMB is left open for diode emulation; above 2.6 V gives fully synchronous operation. VCCDIS is left open so the internal VCC regulators run; above 1.25 V turns them off.

Splitting a high-current output between two identical channels halves each channel's current. Because the channels switch 180° apart, ripple current in the output capacitors is much reduced (most at 50 % duty, less away from it) and the ripple in input and output capacitors appears at twice the switching frequency. Design each phase for half the current with the single-channel equations, then use the output cancellation factor (output capacitor ripple over the ripple in either inductor) and the normalised input RMS ripple against duty cycle to size the capacitors, taking the worst case over the duty-cycle range. Capacitance chosen for ESR may still set the bank size. On the evaluation board, interleaving is enabled by shorting the outputs (with identical power stages), fitting 0 Ω for R21 and R22, and removing C14, R6 and C15.

Two LM25119 devices can make four phases. Feed the RT pins of the master and slave with clocks 90° apart; join all COMP pins; tie the slave channels' FB pins to their local VCC; tie RES to local VCC, which disables hiccup; and join all UVLO pins, which makes the hysteresis current 4 × 20 µA. A VCC or thermal shutdown on the master eventually stops all four channels by pulling the COMP bus down; the same fault on the slave stops only the slave.

The inductor follows from frequency, load, ripple and the input and output voltages; ripple is largest at maximum input. IPP is typically 20 % to 40 % of full load. In diode emulation the peak-to-peak ripple must stay below twice the minimum load current; fully synchronous operation tolerates more. More ripple allows a smaller inductor but loads the output capacitor. Recalculate IPP when the standard value differs much from the calculated one. Check the inductor's saturation current against the short-circuit peak, especially when hot.

Size the output current capability 20 % to 50 % above the required load to cover tolerance and ripple. A larger K lowers sense-resistor loss and cross-talk between channels, which shows as switching jitter. The sense resistor must handle its dissipation at maximum input, when the low-side MOSFET conducts most of the cycle.

The output bank filters the inductor ripple and carries the load through current steps. In the example a 680 µF electrolytic with 10 mΩ ESR is the main capacitor, with two low-ESR/ESL 22 µF ceramics in parallel to cut ripple and spikes.

The input source is typically high-impedance at the switching frequency, so the input capacitors supply most of the pulsed switch current; choose them for RMS rating (IRMS > IOUT / 2) and ripple. Ripple shrinks with both channels running 180° apart. Paralleled capacitors share current by their impedance at the switching frequency, so check each one's rating. The line inductance and input capacitors form a resonant circuit, and the converter presents a negative input impedance, lowest at minimum input; near minimum input on a bench supply a bulk aluminium electrolytic across CIN may be needed for damping.

The VCC capacitor supplies the LO driver and bootstrap diode current peaks, several amperes, and stabilises the regulator: at least 0.47 µF of good low-ESR ceramic at the IC pins (1 µF in the example). The bootstrap capacitor supplies the high-side gate charge and the bootstrap diode's recovery charge: at least 0.1 µF of low-ESR ceramic at the pins (0.47 µF in the example).
Choose RFB1 between 500 Ω and 10 kΩ, large enough that the divider dissipation stays small.

MOSFET choice follows the same trade-offs as frequency; with discrete SO-8 MOSFETs the output current range is generally 2 A to 10 A. Losses split into conduction, gate charging (dissipated in the controller, and more so when the internal regulator supplies the gate current) and switching (high side only, since the low-side body diode conducts before that MOSFET turns on). The MOSFETs must stand the maximum input plus ringing drain to source and VCC plus ringing gate to source. In the 36 V example the SI7884 (7.5 mΩ, 21 nC) is used. With a large step-down ratio, a low-Qg high side and a low-RDS(ON) low side help efficiency.

An RC snubber across the low-side MOSFET damps ringing and spikes at the switch node, which left alone can make the converter misbehave and inject noise into the output. Keep its leads very short, start with 5 Ω to 50 Ω, and choose the smallest capacitor that damps the spikes at high load; more capacitance damps more but loses more. A good layout may not need one.

With current-mode control two parts, RCOMP and CCOMP, close the loop. The loop gain is the modulator gain times the error amplifier gain; the modulator is treated as a voltage-controlled current source with a low-frequency pole set by RLOAD and COUT. RCOMP and CCOMP make a Type II amplifier (80 dB DC gain, an integrator pole and a zero at fZEA); that zero offsets the modulator pole, so the loop falls at one-pole slope and about 90° phase margin at crossover. In the 3.3 V example the crossover target is 11 kHz and the zero must be a decade or more below it. Raising RCOMP while lowering CCOMP in proportion raises the mid-band gain, RCOMP / RFB2. With K between 2 and 3, check stability with a network analyser; without one, use load-step tests aiming for little overshoot and a damped response. CHF adds noise immunity at the cost of a pole that must lie well beyond crossover.
The part runs from a DC source within its input voltage range.

The two regulators run almost independently, but cross-talk between them can show as switch jitter, usually worst when one channel is near 50 % duty. Keep the two high-current loops (input capacitor, high-side and low-side MOSFETs, sense resistor) as small as possible; keep signal and power grounds apart; place the VCC capacitors and the VIN capacitor right at the IC; route CS and CSG side by side as Kelvin lines to the sense resistor; take AGND and PGND directly to the exposed pad; and keep high currents out from under the pad.

Coupling between channels through the input rail: keep the high-current path short, use MOSFETs with low lead inductance, put local bypass capacitors (CIN1, CIN2) right at each high-side MOSFET, slow the switch edges with larger gate resistors (R29, R30) and parallel input capacitors to cut ESR and ESL. High-frequency noise picked up by FB, CS, CSG or COMP: star grounding with short high-current paths, keep signal traces away from SW, HO, HB and the inductor, add an RC filter between CS and CSG, and put its capacitor (C30, C31) beside the IC on the same layer. Ground shift at the switching frequency: star grounding with a short distance between the grounds of CIN1 and CIN2.

In the recommended layout the ground is a solid plane joined in a star; the high-current paths are as wide and short as possible; small-signal traces may be narrow but stay clear of radiated and capacitively coupled noise; and the input bypass points at each channel get the most high-frequency decoupling, isolating each channel from the other's switching noise. The feedback resistors sit near the IC on the AGND side.
The part has limited built-in ESD protection; store and handle it with leads shorted or in conductive foam to protect the MOS gates.
